write_command has already refused any opening outside the limits by more than a nanometre (the range check above it), so the value that reaches the conversion is inside [low, high] to within 1e-9 m, which is three millionths of a register: the clamp changes no register, and the maker's own conversion clamps to the profile besides.

the manager clears every component it had loaded when one fails to initialize (F137), so the declared-component lookup that follows refuses the same body for the same reason; the clause only changes which component the message names, and no caller can tell

`parse_control_resources_from_urdf` throws on a document with no <ros2_control> element, and the catch above this check refuses it; the empty-list branch is unreachable with this framework's parser (it is kept for a parser that returns an empty list instead), so no URDF can reach it

the arrays are rebuilt at the end of every successful `_open` before anything reads them, and a refused one leaves `_travel` empty (it is reset in the same place), so a command raises on the travel lookup before it reaches the hold arrays: what a reader of the old arrays could see, it cannot reach. A refused reopen of a bridge that was never closed also leaves `_opened` true, which no caller can reach through the python-host (each open there is a fresh child, torn down on refusal) and is recorded in the fifty-seventh session's entry rather than fixed

the seeded values are never read: a hold target is assigned from the measured position (or the last setpoint) the first time a joint is held, before it is used, and `_setpoint` is read only for a joint whose `_have_setpoint` is set, which is set by the write that assigns it. The behaviour this seed is about, a never-commanded joint held at its measured position and not at the zero the arrays were sized with, is asserted by the suite and killed by `piper-hold-start-zero-first`

`Bus.send` of the loopback bus and of the kernel's CAN socket return after queuing, and the commit follows on the next statement, so no caller can observe the order: a send that raised would propagate out of write_command in either order, and the next write recomputes every hold from the committed state it was left

a stop that finds no bus is a stop on a body that was never opened or has been closed, and after close() every read and write refuses with EPERM on `_opened` before `_estop` is read, so the latch it would have set can never refuse anything the closed session does not already

the stamp is read from a monotonic clock and the loopback bus delivers inside the same call, so the only difference between the two orders is a few microseconds of Python that no assertion about a stamp (monotonic, advancing, not in the future) can tell apart
